source_title: Mississippi Unmanned Aircraft Systems Protection Act of 2021
revision_date: None identified since original 2021 enactment; brought forward without substantive change in subsequent session bills (e.g., 2024 HB 1370, 2025 HB 1494) that separately failed
uas_topic: Critical-infrastructure / correctional-facility UAS restriction; law enforcement/public-agency UAS use
regulated_party: Any individual (§ 97-47-5); public agencies and public contractors other than law enforcement (§ 97-47-7)
regulated_activity: Using a UAS to conduct surveillance of, collect information/data from, or photographically/electronically record a 'critical infrastructure' (petroleum refinery/tank farm, electrical generation facility supporting the MS power grid, natural gas processing/terminal facility, military installation, or DOD/State Military Department contractor) or a 'correctional facility' (state, federal, municipal/county, or youth detention) without prior written consent of the owner or designee; separately, delivering or attempting to deliver contraband to a correctional facility by UAS
requirement_type: Prohibition with consent-based exception for surveillance/recording; public-agency/public-contractor operation requires written consent of the critical-infrastructure/correctional-facility owner plus FAA compliance
permit_or_approval_required: Written consent of the owner or owner's designee of the critical infrastructure or correctional facility (no form or process specified in the statute)
public_agency_only: No (applies to any individual; a separate, narrower consent-and-FAA-compliance rule applies to public agencies/contractors under § 97-47-7)
aec_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to any AEC firm performing inspection, mapping, or construction-monitoring UAS work at or near Mississippi petroleum/tank-farm, power-generation, gas-processing, military, or correctional facilities
summary: Miss. Code Ann. § 97-47-5 makes it an offense to knowingly (a) use a UAS to conduct surveillance of, collect information or data from, or photographically/electronically record a 'critical infrastructure' or 'correctional facility' (both narrowly defined at § 97-47-3) without the prior written consent of the owner or owner's designee, or (b) deliver or attempt to deliver contraband by UAS onto correctional-facility property or adjacent property. Section 97-47-9 makes a violation of (a) a misdemeanor (up to 1 year and/or a $1,000 fine) and a violation of (b) a felony (3-15 years and/or a $25,000 fine). Section 97-47-7 exempts law-enforcement UAS use for any lawful purpose and permits other public agencies/public contractors to operate a UAS over such sites only with the facility owner's written consent and in accordance with FAA rules; the chapter does not apply to UAS operating under an FAA Certificate of Waiver or Authorization. 'Critical infrastructure' is defined narrowly (petroleum refinery/tank farm; power-generation facility supporting the Mississippi grid; natural gas processing/terminal facility; federal/state military installation; DOD/State Military Department contractor) and does NOT extend to water/wastewater plants, telecommunications, ports, or rail/freight facilities as some secondary sources claim (see notes).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Map the statute's specifically defined critical-infrastructure and correctional-facility boundaries before planning the sensor footprint, and obtain prior written owner or designee consent for covered collection. Keep delivery devices and loose payloads out of correctional-facility missions, with lost-link and emergency procedures designed to prevent entry or delivery onto the facility or adjacent property.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: The facility owner or designee should provide a written consent route that identifies the covered site, operator, aircraft, pilots, dates, collection purpose, sensor limits, data recipients, and field contact. Public agencies and contractors should also preserve FAA-compliance evidence and the facility owner's consent rather than treating a project assignment as implicit authorization.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: For correctional-facility work, use configuration control for payload mounts, release mechanisms, return-to-home, and lost-link behavior so the aircraft cannot inadvertently deliver an object onto covered or adjacent property. Procurement should also support geospatial mission boundaries and auditable sensor settings, but those controls do not replace written owner consent.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the signed facility-owner or designee consent, proof of the signer's authority, boundary map, mission and sensor limits, FAA status, and all amendments. Escalate whether a site meets the statute's narrow definitions, whether adjacent property is implicated, or whether a proposed payload could be characterized as contraband delivery before flight.
verification_status: §§ 97-47-1, 97-47-3, 97-47-7, and 97-47-9 were each fetched and read in full directly from law.justia.com (official Mississippi Code text). § 97-47-5 itself could not be directly rendered by the fetch tool after repeated attempts, but its exact current text was independently cross-verified as identical, word-for-word, across four separate primary sources: three official Mississippi Legislature bill-drafting texts that each 'bring forward' or quote § 97-47-5 verbatim (2023 HB 839, 2024 HB 1370, 2025 HB 1494, all at billstatus.ls.state.ms.us) and a direct Justia search-engine excerpt of the same section.
notes: CITATION-DISCREPANCY FLAG: a secondary AI-generated summary (from a general web search) asserted that 'critical infrastructure' under this chapter includes 'water and wastewater plants, telecommunications infrastructure, ports, and rail and freight facilities.' This is INCORRECT — the primary text of § 97-47-3(b), fetched directly, defines 'critical infrastructure' narrowly as only: petroleum refinery/tank farm; MS-grid-supporting electrical generation facility; natural gas processing/terminal facility; military installation; and DOD/State Military Department contractor. The broader secondary description appears to conflate this chapter with a different critical-infrastructure trespass statute or another state's law and is not used in this record.

source_title: Uncrewed Aircraft Systems' Rights and Authorities Act
revision_date: None identified; current codified text matches original 2023 enactment (later 2024/2025 amendment bills, HB 1370 and HB 1494, both died in committee — see notes)
uas_topic: State preemption of local UAS regulation; recreational/commercial UAS operation authorization; UAS civil/criminal liability
regulated_party: Individuals and business entities operating UAS recreationally or commercially; political subdivisions of the state
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS recreationally or commercially within Mississippi; a political subdivision enacting or enforcing a UAS-specific ordinance
requirement_type: Statutory authorization (operators) coupled with state preemption of most local UAS ordinances (political subdivisions), subject to enumerated exceptions
public_agency_only: No (state-level statute; also directly limits political subdivisions, i.e., local governments)
aec_relevance: Yes — establishes Mississippi's statewide preemption posture and confirms no additional state UAS registration is required beyond FAA rules, both material to multi-jurisdiction AEC UAS project planning
summary: Miss. Code Ann. § 61-21-5 authorizes an individual, in compliance with federal law, to operate a UAS recreationally, and an individual or business entity doing business lawfully in the state to operate/use a UAS commercially, and provides that a UAS owner is not required to register the aircraft beyond what federal law requires. § 61-21-7 provides that a person is liable for an act or offense committed with the aid of a UAS if the conduct would have given rise to civil or criminal liability had it been performed directly, and that a UAS can be the instrumentality of a privacy-rights tort. § 61-21-9 (the preemption provision) bars a political subdivision from enacting or enforcing an ordinance relating to UAS ownership, operation, design, manufacture, testing, maintenance, licensing, registration, certification, airspace, altitude, flight paths, equipment, or pilot/operator/observer qualifications, subject to exceptions allowing a political subdivision to: enforce FAA restrictions; regulate its own government-owned/operated UAS; enforce generally applicable (non-UAS-specific) nuisance, voyeurism, harassment, trespass, reckless-endangerment, or property-damage ordinances; and regulate UAS launch/landing/pilot-presence on political-subdivision-owned property. § 61-21-9(3) separately clarifies the Act does not prohibit UAS takeoff/landing for emergency or critical-infrastructure maintenance support, technical-malfunction landings, sworn public-safety-officer operations, or federal-government operations.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Use the state preemption rule to screen UAS-specific local restrictions, but still check generally applicable nuisance, voyeurism, harassment, trespass, and property-damage rules and the public owner's launch, landing, and pilot-location conditions. Record the route, launch and landing rights, emergency or maintenance basis if used, and any non-UAS-specific site restrictions in the flight packet.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Do not describe Mississippi preemption as eliminating all local or property controls; the Act preserves enumerated ordinances and public-property authority and leaves ordinary liability intact. Escalate novel local UAS restrictions, privacy-intensive collection, or reliance on an emergency, malfunction, infrastructure-maintenance, or public-safety landing protection.
verification_status: Chapter listing plus §§ 61-21-5 and 61-21-9 fetched and read in full directly from law.justia.com (official Mississippi Code text); enactment vehicle (2023 SB 2146, ch. 306) confirmed via the codified History note.
notes: Two subsequent bills (2024 HB 1370, passed House 108-7 but died in Senate Judiciary Division A on 2024-04-02; 2025 HB 1494, died in House Judiciary A on 2025-02-04) would have added language to § 61-21-5 conditioning recreational operation on not otherwise violating state law and would have added UAS-specific surveillance language to the general trespass statutes (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 97-17-85, 97-17-87, 97-17-93, 97-17-97) and to the licensed-surveyor land-entry statute (§ 73-13-103). NEITHER BILL WAS ENACTED; the general trespass statutes and § 73-13-103 currently contain NO UAS-specific language. This is flagged because secondary sources and even legislative bill captions can create a false impression that these amendments are current law — they are not. See Non-Regulatory Context in the printable summary.

issuing_authority: Mississippi Legislature; state public-procurement framework administered under Title 31, Chapter 7
source_title: State-Purchased Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems — Domestic Manufacturer, Collision-Avoidance, and Country-of-Origin Requirements
effective_date: 2023-07-01 (Laws, 2023, ch. 460, § 1); amended by Laws, 2024, ch. 498, § 2, eff. 2024-07-01; substantive domestic-manufacturer/China-ban provisions effective 2025-01-01
uas_topic: State UAS procurement, manufacturer, and country-of-origin restriction
regulated_party: State of Mississippi and its agencies and political subdivisions (as purchasers); domestic manufacturers and domestic sUAS maintenance/repair companies (as bid-preference beneficiaries)
regulated_activity: Purchasing, operating, maintaining, or repairing a small UAS ('sUAS') on behalf of the state or a political subdivision; contracting for state infrastructure-inspection services requiring sUAS use
requirement_type: Domestic-sourcing mandate; China-manufacture ban (with grandfather exception); in-state bid preference
permit_or_approval_required: Not applicable in the permit sense — this is a procurement sourcing/eligibility requirement, not an approval process
public_agency_only: Yes — applies to the State of Mississippi and its agencies and political subdivisions as purchasers, not directly to a private AEC consultant's own equipment (see notes on contract flow-down)
commercial_operator_relevance: Indirect — governs what the state/political subdivisions may purchase and what a state-contracted infrastructure-inspection sUAS provider must use, rather than private commercial operation generally
aec_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to any AEC firm bidding on or delivering Mississippi public-agency UAS infrastructure-inspection work, and to any firm selling or maintaining sUAS to Mississippi public entities
summary: Miss. Code Ann. § 31-7-67(2) requires that, beginning January 1, 2025, all sUAS purchased by the State of Mississippi or any agency/political subdivision be purchased exclusively from a 'domestic manufacturer' (U.S.-incorporated and headquartered, majority American-owned, manufacturing in the U.S.), possess a collision-avoidance system, and have all maintenance/repair/technical services performed by a 'domestic sUAS company'; it further requires that all state-contracted infrastructure-inspection services requiring sUAS use employ domestically manufactured sUAS. Subsection (3) grants domestic Mississippi-based manufacturers and sUAS companies a 10% bid preference over non-Mississippi competitors in Title 31, Chapter 7 procurement, and requires agencies to solicit at least one bid from a Mississippi-based sUAS manufacturer. Subsection (4) bars an agency from purchasing or operating an sUAS manufactured in the People's Republic of China, defined to include assembly outside China using more than a negligible amount of PRC-origin parts, software, components, or raw materials. Subsection (5) exempts a state institution of higher learning with a federally designated research center conducting sUAS research, and subsection (6) grandfathers PRC-manufactured sUAS purchased before January 1, 2025.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: For state-contracted infrastructure inspection, confirm at proposal and aircraft-assignment stages that the consultant-furnished sUAS meets the domestic-manufacturer requirement expressly applied to that service. Keep the public client's purchase and operation rules distinct from an ordinary private project, while treating any incorporated aircraft, collision-avoidance, service, or origin term as a mobilization gate.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Purchasing staff should document domestic-manufacturer status, collision-avoidance capability, required Mississippi bid solicitation and preference, maintenance-provider eligibility, country-of-origin review, and any research or grandfather basis. For infrastructure-inspection contracts, state the aircraft-eligibility requirement expressly and verify the proposed model and configuration before notice to proceed.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Obtain traceable evidence of U.S. incorporation, headquarters, ownership, manufacturing, component and software origin, collision-avoidance capability, and domestic maintenance support before offering a system for covered work. Recheck eligibility at solicitation, award, and deployment, and maintain a replacement plan because a generic 'assembled in the USA' claim does not establish the statute's PRC-content or domestic-manufacturer tests.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Define whether the transaction is a public purchase, public operation, covered state infrastructure-inspection service, grandfathered aircraft, or research-institution use, because the obligations differ. Retain manufacturer and origin attestations, bid records, aircraft configuration, service-provider qualifications, and the contract clause that creates any consultant flow-down.
verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from law.justia.com (official Mississippi Code text), including the History note confirming the 2023 enactment and 2024 amendment.
notes: This statute binds the state and its agencies/political subdivisions as purchasers and, for infrastructure-inspection services, extends the domestic-sUAS requirement to the contracted service itself; it does not, on its face, restrict equipment a private AEC firm may own or use for non-state work. Whether a specific public contract's terms flow this requirement down to a consultant's own fleet must be confirmed against the individual contract/RFP, consistent with the project's procurement-interpretation guardrails.

issuing_authority: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks (MDWFP); Mississippi Commission on Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks
source_title: Basic Regulations for All Wildlife Management Areas — Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Launch/Landing Prohibition
effective_date: Unknown — rule has been amended repeatedly; UAV-specific provision (GG) present in the version current through the most recent quarterly update reviewed
revision_date: Amended 7/25/2024 (most recent amendment date shown on the rule as accessed)
uas_topic: UAS use on state wildlife management area land
regulated_party: Any person on an MDWFP-owned Wildlife Management Area
regulated_activity: Launching or landing a UAV on MDWFP-owned WMA land
requirement_type: Prohibition (launch/landing only; the rule text does not separately address overflight)
commercial_operator_relevance: No direct commercial-operator-specific requirement — the launch/landing prohibition applies to any person, including commercial operators, on MDWFP-owned WMA land
aec_relevance: Yes — relevant to AEC/environmental-consulting firms conducting mapping, inspection, or environmental-monitoring UAS work that would require launching or landing on an MDWFP-owned WMA
summary: 40 Miss. Code R. 2-1.1, the basic regulations applicable to all Mississippi Wildlife Management Areas, provides at subsection (GG): 'Unmanned Aerial Vehicles may not be launched from or landed on MDWFP-Owned Wildlife Management Areas.' The rule is issued under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 39-7-11, 49-1-29, 49-4-4, and 49-5-13, and is not itself the general hunting-harassment statute; it exists alongside numerous other WMA use restrictions (target shooting, ORV/vehicle use, hunter-orange requirements, etc.) in the same consolidated rule.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan launch and recovery outside MDWFP-owned WMA land and map the property boundary, alternate landing sites, return-to-home point, and lost-link behavior accordingly. The rule addresses launch and landing rather than overflight, but site access and wildlife or hunting conditions still require separate screening.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Preserve the ownership boundary, launch and landing coordinates, site-access rights, route, return-to-home and emergency-landing plan, and incident log. Do not recast the rule as a general WMA overflight ban, and escalate a mission that lacks a lawful off-property recovery option.
verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from the Cornell Legal Information Institute's Mississippi Administrative Code database, which mirrors the Mississippi Secretary of State's official rule text; rule text explicitly uses the terms 'Unmanned Aerial Vehicles.'
notes: The rule restricts only launch/landing, not overflight, of WMA land; a mission that transits WMA airspace without launching or landing there would not, on the face of this rule alone, be restricted by subsection (GG), though other WMA provisions (e.g., wildlife-harassment prohibitions) could still be implicated.

source_title: Alligator Hunting Season Regulations — Drone/UAV Prohibition
citation: 40 Miss. Code R. 2-5.2 (private lands), 2-5.3 (public waters), and 2-5.4 (Pelahatchie Bay)
effective_date: Unknown — underlying rules amended annually; drone/UAV provision confirmed in the version of 2-5.3 current as accessed (noted by the publisher as effective until 7/1/2025, with a successor version not independently verified in this pass)
revision_date: Amended 5/23/2022 (most recent amendment shown for 2-5.3 as accessed)
status: Current / in force (see notes on successor-version currency)
binding_level: Binding (administrative rule); Class III violation for breach
regulated_party: Persons hunting or assisting in the hunting of American alligator under an MDWFP Alligator Possession Permit
regulated_activity: Using a drone, UAV, or other remotely operated vehicle/vessel to assist in locating, pursuing, or taking an alligator
permit_or_approval_required: No (applies within an already-permitted alligator hunt; does not itself create a separate UAS permit)
commercial_operator_relevance: No direct commercial-operator-specific requirement — applies to any person assisting in an alligator hunt, whether recreational or otherwise
aec_relevance: Limited (relevant primarily to recreational/regulated alligator-hunting activity rather than typical AEC commercial operations; relevant if an AEC/environmental-monitoring UAS mission is conducted in or near an active alligator-hunting zone during the open season)
summary: 40 Miss. Code R. 2-5.3(E)(3)(p) (public-waters alligator season) states: 'The use of drones, UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles), or any remotely operated vehicle or vessel to assist in the location, pursuit, and/or take of alligators is prohibited.' Materially identical language appears in the companion private-lands (2-5.2) and Pelahatchie Bay (2-5.4) alligator-season rules. A violation of this provision is a Class III violation under Miss. Code Ann. § 49-7-101. The rule is issued under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 49-1-29, 49-4-4, and 49-7-47.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Screen the mission for active hunting and wildlife sensitivity within Statewide (public waters, private lands, and Pelahatchie Bay alligator-hunting zones); plan altitude, stand-off distance, route, observers, and abort criteria to avoid pursuit, harassment, surveillance of participants, or assistance to a taking. Document the project's environmental or infrastructure purpose and pause if animals materially react or the flight would disrupt lawful hunting or fishing.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the legitimate project purpose, alligator-hunting-season and zone screening, route, communications, and any coordination with hunters or land managers. Stop and escalate any request to use imagery or live location data to locate, pursue, or take alligators, even if the requester holds an Alligator Possession Permit.
verification_status: 40 Miss. Code R. 2-5.3 fetched and read in full directly from the Cornell Legal Information Institute's Mississippi Administrative Code database; the publisher labels the fetched version '[Effective until 7/1/2025],' indicating a successor version exists for the current (2025-2026) alligator season whose exact text — including whether the drone prohibition is retained verbatim — was not independently re-fetched and confirmed in this pass.
notes: Confidence rated Moderate rather than High solely due to the unconfirmed successor-version text; the drone/UAV prohibition has been a stable, recurring feature of Mississippi's annual alligator-season rules across multiple amendment cycles reviewed, making a substantive repeal unlikely but not independently verified for the current season.

issuing_authority: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks (MDWFP)
source_title: General Rules and Regulations for State Parks — Aircraft Operation Restriction
effective_date: Unknown — rule amended on an ongoing basis; provision confirmed current through June 12, 2025 per the version accessed
uas_topic: UAS use on state park land
regulated_party: Any person on Mississippi State Park property
regulated_activity: Operating an aircraft on land or water, or air-delivering a person or thing by parachute, helicopter, hot-air balloon, or other means, on state park property
requirement_type: Prohibition subject to a written-permission exception
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — written permission of the Executive Director of MDWFP (no application form, fee, or processing time specified in the rule; applicants should confirm process directly with MDWFP)
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — applies to any person on state park property, including commercial AEC operators, not only recreational visitors
aec_relevance: Yes — relevant to AEC firms performing mapping, inspection, or construction-documentation UAS work within a Mississippi State Park
summary: 40 Miss. Code R. 6-1.2(W)(18) provides: 'Except in an extreme emergency, the operation of aircraft on land or water or the air delivery of any person or thing by parachute, helicopter, hot air balloon or other means, without the written permission of the Executive Director of the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks, is prohibited.' The rule text itself does not use the words 'drone' or 'unmanned aircraft,' but the prohibition is framed in terms of 'aircraft' generally, and secondary MDWFP-sourced guidance describes park drone use as requiring the same written special-use-permit process administered by park management/the Executive Director. The rule is issued under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 49-1-29, 49-4-4, and 55-3-33.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat property authorization for State park lands managed by MDWFP statewide as a pre-mobilization gate and obtain conditions that cover launch, landing, route, dates, aircraft, crew, and sensor purpose. Confirm whether the approval is site-wide or location-specific and carry the written authorization and field contact with the crew.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Route the request to MDWFP for written Executive Director permission and identify the state park, operating and recovery areas, dates, aircraft, pilots, purpose, payload, insurance, emergency plan, and field contact. Because the rule supplies no form, fee, or dependable review time, confirm the current submission method and lead time directly rather than inventing a standard process.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the request, written Executive Director permission, proof of scope and conditions, property map, insurance, amendments, and park communications. Confirm in writing that the approval covers the UAS operation and any air delivery or payload activity rather than relying on a client's general access direction.
verification_status: Rule 40-6-1.2 fetched and read in full directly (Justia's Mississippi Administrative Code mirror, current through June 12, 2025). Confidence rated Moderate rather than High because the rule text itself addresses 'aircraft' generally rather than naming 'drone' or 'unmanned aircraft' specifically; the drone-specific application rests on MDWFP's general 'aircraft' framing plus consistent secondary reporting rather than an express UAS reference in the rule text.

summary: Miss. Code Ann. § 49-7-147 currently prohibits intentionally (a) interfering with or attempting to prevent another's lawful taking of wildlife, (b) attempting to disturb wildlife or affect its behavior with intent to prevent another's lawful taking of it, or (c) harassing a person engaged in lawful taking of wildlife or preparation for such taking; a violation is a Class II violation under Miss. Code Ann. § 49-7-143. The currently codified text contains NO reference to drones, UAS, or unmanned aircraft. A bill (House Bill 719, apparently introduced in an earlier session) proposed amending this section specifically to prohibit using an unmanned system to conduct video surveillance of, or interfere with, a person engaged in lawful hunting or fishing; that amendment was not confirmed enacted, and the current codified section (verified directly) does not contain it.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Screen the mission for active hunting and wildlife sensitivity within Statewide (wherever wild animals are taken or pursued); plan altitude, stand-off distance, route, observers, and abort criteria to avoid pursuit, harassment, surveillance of participants, or assistance to a taking. Document the project's environmental or infrastructure purpose and pause if animals materially react or the flight would disrupt lawful hunting or fishing.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Preserve the legitimate project purpose, active-hunting and fishing screening, route, timing, wildlife response, communications, and any complaint or stop-work action. The current statute is not UAS-specific, so focus the analysis on intentional interference, disturbance, or harassment rather than implying that ordinary project imagery is categorically prohibited.
